extracted.intended_audience: public relations students, corporate public affairs practitioners, and government-relations professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative measures for corporate public affairs and community-relations programs, including metrics to evaluate communication efforts, typical functions and structures of public affairs units, techniques used to manage issues, and the duties of Washington representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of local governmental officials reporting contact
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of local governmental officials reporting contact with community relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic quantitative measure of outreach to government officials; used to assess the extent of contact between the organization and local government actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of members of local publics reporting contact
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of members of local publics—interest groups or 'constituencies'—reporting contact with community relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts contacts with nonleader members of local publics; indicates breadth of community reach beyond elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of community leaders reporting discussion of controversial/policy issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of community leaders who report having discussed controversial or policy issues with community relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure should be augmented with open-ended questions on what was discussed during contacts with representatives to capture substance of interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of community leaders who understand the organization’s position
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of community leaders who understand the organization’s position on controversial or policy questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure message retention using question formats described in Chapter 9 (e.g., recall/understanding items) to assess whether messages were comprehended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of community leaders reporting they gave information to representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of community leaders who report giving information to community relations representatives about service or community problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-ended questions to elicit the kinds of information leaders provided; this gauges two-way flow and community problem-identification role of the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of organizational managers reporting receipt of community information
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of organizational managers who report having received information about service or community problems from community relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures internal transmission of community-sourced information to managerial decisionmakers; useful for assessing organizational feedback loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of managers reporting policy or behavior changes from received information
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of managers reporting that they have made changes in policy or behavior as a result of the information received about service or community problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct measure of impact on organizational decisions and practices attributable to community relations input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of negative behaviors reported by community leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of negative behaviors reported by community leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chapter 9 for question designs to measure behavior; this metric tracks adverse actions toward the organization (e.g., protests, boycotts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of negative behaviors directed toward organization versus through outside groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of negative behaviors directed toward the organization rather than through outside groups or agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes direct community backlash from actions channeled via external organizations; useful to understand locus of hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings of extent organization helped solve leaders' top community problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratings by community leaders of the extent to which the organization has helped to solve the three most important community problems defined by each leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate community involvement projects; methodology drawn from Grunig’s second study—eliciting leader-defined problems then asking leader ratings of organizational contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working definition of public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs: 'the management function responsible for interpreting the corporation’s non-commercial environment and managing the company’s response to those factors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to differentiate public affairs (policy/government orientation) from narrower notions of publicity or information dissemination; alternative practical view narrows it to political education and government relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Affairs Council: typical departmental functions and subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical public affairs department has four major functions with subdivisions: Government relations (federal, state, local; political action; PACs; political education; grassroots; communications on political issues); Community involvement/corporate responsibility (community relations, philanthropy, social-responsibility programs, volunteerism); International (political risk assessment, monitoring international socio-political developments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to audit or design a public affairs unit; it indicates the range of responsibilities often housed under 'public affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs core activities (Boston University study)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs centers around two activities—community relations (84.9%) and government relations (84.2%)—with significant responsibility also for corporate contributions (71.5%) and media relations (70.0%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percentages indicate prevalence of responsibilities among surveyed corporate public affairs units and can be used as benchmarking targets for scope of function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs activities that influence corporate planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities include: identify public issues for corporate attention; set or help set priorities for these issues; identify issues for department/division/subsidiary attention; set or help set priorities at those levels; provide forecasts of social/political trends to corporate planning office and to departments/divisions/subsidiaries; review corporate plans for sensitivity to emerging social/political trends; prepare narrative sections regarding future social/political trends included with directions for corporate plans; review department/division/subsidiary plans for sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete functions public affairs units perform to integrate external socio-political intelligence into corporate strategy; percentages of respondents performing each were reported in the Boston University study and can guide role expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques used to manage emerging issues (ranked)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques (mean rank shown in study): Monitor emerging issues (4.1); Lobby within trade associations (4.0); Scan to detect emerging issues (3.9); Communicate company position to managers (3.9); Lobby at the federal level (3.9); Lobby at state/local levels (3.9); Communicate company position to government agencies (3.9); Communicate company positions to employees (3.4); Use issue manager (3.1); Change company information systems (3.0); Change company policies (2.9); Use interdepartmental public affairs issue research committees (2.9); Communicate positions to the general public (2.9); Change company or subunit objectives (2.9); Communicate positions to stockholders (2.9); Change reward and penalty systems (2.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative ordering suggests a predominance of lobbying/monitoring and internal communication activities; use the listed techniques and their ranked importance as a toolkit and to assess whether a program is weighted toward asymmetric vs. symmetric two-way models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of asymmetric vs. symmetric public affairs campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetric (reactive) campaigns use conflict/polarization metaphors and aim to press positions; symmetric (proactive) campaigns use negotiation/bargaining metaphors, aiming for compromise and mutual adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for evaluating campaign strategy: identify whether the program is reactive (polarizing) or proactive (negotiating) and the likely democratic/public-good consequences of each approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common organizational structures for public affairs programs (IBM typology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common structures: (1) A Washington office that interacts with federal government but does not carry on other public affairs functions; (2) A public affairs program located outside Washington that conducts research/analysis and reports to management (writing speeches, etc.), separate from Washington group; (3) Public affairs and government relations merged and located in the Washington office, reporting to management similarly to (2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these archetypes when designing organization structure; examples: IBM uses the merged Washington model, AT&T separates public affairs with a separate VP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational/background composition for public affairs staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Most common backgrounds of public affairs specialists: law; public affairs (community/social affairs, communications, public relations); government (elected/appointed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring signals reflect organizational philosophy: communications-oriented units hire public-affairs/PR-trained people; companies focused on regulatory matters tend to recruit lawyers; issues-management roles attract political scientists and economists. Recommendation: students should include economics and political science in PR training and consider joint degrees (e.g., law + PR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways corporations conduct government relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include: open a Washington government relations office; handle Washington operations from the home office (commuting when necessary); rely totally on trade associations; hire Washington-based consultants (legal, PR, political/economic firms); or use a combination of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston University study frequencies provide benchmarks (e.g., trade association 67.8%, frequent visits to Washington by senior executives 58.4%, company office in Washington 42.7%, Washington law firm 38.0%, government relations counsel 11.9%, Washington PR firm 8.6%). Use these to plan/resourcing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of government Washington representatives work with
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington representatives work with three areas of government: the legislative branch (key legislators and congressional staffs), the executive/administrative departments (e.g., Commerce, Labor, Transportation, HHS), and regulatory agencies (e.g., EPA, FTC, FCC, SEC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation of effort across these areas should reflect corporate objectives; most company government-relations effort concentrates on the legislative branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-finding (Washington rep communication activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-finding: providing the organization with advance information on what government policies or rules are in the making; offices often operate like a news bureau covering beats (Congress, agencies) and communicate via newsletters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by the timeliness, completeness, and relevance of information delivered to internal audiences; often operationalized as monitoring systems and regular briefings/newsletters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liaison (Washington rep communication activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liaison: making personal contacts to exchange information with government officials, reporters, members of professional societies, or scientists; attending hearings, interviewing officials, calling on congressional and agency staff, talking with trade executives; entertaining is an important part of this function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by quality and frequency of contacts, access achieved, and the representative’s ability to exchange actionable information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of government action to management (Washington rep activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting results of fact-finding and liaison for management—explaining legislation, regulation, or ruling and analyzing what action might be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess by clarity, timeliness, and decision-relevance of analyses provided to managers; includes recommended courses of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information giving (Washington rep communication activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information flows from Washington representatives to government: providing statistical data or market information and explaining the effect that legislation or rules being considered might have on the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by the completeness and persuasiveness of information provided to agencies/officials and by the extent to which it influences regulatory framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy (Washington rep communication activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy: when fact-finding or liaison indicates action is necessary, the representative recommends lobbying, grassroots campaigns, or communication campaigns; may coordinate persuasive efforts, bring in experts/technicians/consultants/executives to testify or meet with legislators. Representatives who spend majority of time influencing legislation must register as lobbyists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess advocacy by strategy selection (lobbying, grassroots, coalition-building), coordination effectiveness, compliance with lobbying regulations, and outcome metrics (legislative/regulatory results).
